tips.title: BMI divides by height squared
tips.body: $\text{BMI} = \dfrac{\text{mass in kg}}{(\text{height in m})^2}$. Dividing by the height once instead of squaring it is the standard slip, and it makes every BMI far too large.

tips.title: Correlation is not cause
tips.body: Data showing smokers get more heart disease shows a **correlation**. Saying it **causes** it needs a mechanism as well. Write "is a risk factor for" unless the question gives you the biology.

tips.title: Risk factors interact
tips.body: Diet, exercise, alcohol and smoking are not independent. A question asking why one person is at more risk usually wants **two or more** factors and how they combine.

steps.title: Many causes, not one
steps.body:
A **non-communicable disease** cannot be caught. It usually has no single cause: it comes from the **interaction of a number of factors**.

- **Genes** you inherit.
- **Lifestyle**: diet, exercise, smoking, alcohol.
- **Environment**: air pollution, where you live and work.
- **Age**: the risk of most of these diseases rises with age.

Each one is a **risk factor**: something that makes a disease *more likely*, not certain. The specification names the main groups: **cardiovascular diseases**, many forms of **cancer**, some **lung** and **liver** diseases, and diseases influenced by **nutrition**.

rows: smoking, diet high in fat, lack of exercise
props.title: Risk factors, not single causes

visuals.alt: A table of the main non-communicable diseases and some of the risk factors for each

check.solution: A risk factor makes a disease **more likely**, not certain.
options: something that makes a disease more likely
something that always causes a disease
a pathogen that causes a disease
a treatment that prevents a disease

steps.title: Diet, exercise, obesity and malnutrition
steps.body:
If you take in more **energy** from food than you use, the extra is stored as fat. Over time that leads to **obesity**, which raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and some cancers. **Exercise** uses energy and so helps keep the balance.

**Malnutrition** is not just *too little food*. It means a diet without the right balance: too little energy or too little of a nutrient (such as a vitamin or protein), or too much. In some places people cannot get enough food; in others they eat far more energy than they use. Both are forms of malnutrition.

visuals.alt: A table comparing obesity and undernutrition, their causes and effects

check.solution: **Malnutrition** is an unbalanced diet — too little *or* too much of something.

markScheme.description: a diet without the right balance

options: a diet without the right balance of nutrients
eating any amount of fatty food
not taking enough exercise
being below a healthy weight only

steps.title: Calculating BMI
steps.body:
**Body mass index** (BMI) compares mass with height:

**BMI = mass (kg) ÷ height (m)²**

Square the height first, then divide. The NHS uses these bands for adults: **below 18.5** underweight; **18.5 to 24.9** healthy weight; **25 to 29.9** overweight; **30 or more** obese.

BMI has a limit: it only uses mass and height, so it cannot tell **muscle from fat**.

visuals.problem: A person has a mass of 72 kg and a height of 1.80 m. Find their BMI.
Rearranging: what mass gives a BMI of 25 at 1.80 m?

check.prompt: A person has a mass of 81 kg and a height of 1.80 m. Calculate their BMI.

steps.title: Waist-to-hip ratio
steps.body:
The **waist-to-hip ratio** shows *where* fat is stored:

**waist-to-hip ratio = waist circumference ÷ hip circumference**

Measure both in the same units, so they cancel and the ratio has none. A higher ratio means more fat around the abdomen, and fat stored there is linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. An exam question will give you any values to compare against.

visuals.problem: Waist 90 cm, hips 100 cm. Find the ratio.

check.prompt: Waist 76 cm, hips 95 cm. Calculate the waist-to-hip ratio.

steps.title: Alcohol and the liver
steps.body:
The **liver** breaks down alcohol, which is a **toxin**. Drinking too much over many years damages and kills liver cells.

- At first fat builds up in the liver.
- Damaged cells are replaced by **scar tissue**: this is **cirrhosis**, and a scarred liver cannot do its jobs properly.
- The risk of **liver cancer** rises.

Alcohol is a risk factor, not a certain cause: how much damage it does depends on how much and how long, and on other factors such as genes.

visuals.problem: How does heavy drinking lead to liver disease?

steps.text: The liver breaks down alcohol, a toxin
Over years, liver cells are damaged and killed
They are replaced by scar tissue: **cirrhosis**
So the liver cannot work properly, and the risk of liver cancer rises

check.prompt: What name is given to scarring of the liver caused by long-term heavy drinking?

steps.title: Smoking and cardiovascular disease
steps.body:
**Cardiovascular disease** is disease of the heart and blood vessels. Smoking raises the risk in several ways.

- Chemicals in smoke **damage the lining of the arteries**. **Fatty deposits** build up at the damage and narrow the arteries.
- **Nicotine** raises heart rate and **blood pressure**, which damages the arteries further.
- **Carbon monoxide** reduces how much oxygen the blood can carry, so the heart has to work harder.

If the **coronary arteries**, which supply the heart muscle, narrow or are blocked by a clot, part of the heart muscle gets no oxygen: a **heart attack**. A clot that blocks an artery to the brain causes a **stroke**.

rows: damage artery lining, fatty deposits build
raises heart rate and blood pressure
less oxygen carried, heart works harder
props.title: How smoking harms the heart

visuals.alt: A table of the chemicals in cigarette smoke and how each raises the risk of cardiovascular disease

check.prompt: What happens when a coronary artery is blocked?
check.solution: The coronary arteries supply the **heart muscle**; without blood it gets no oxygen and cells die: a heart attack.
options: heart muscle gets no oxygen, a heart attack
the lungs cannot take in oxygen
the liver cannot break down toxins
the kidneys stop filtering the blood

steps.title: Local, national and global
steps.body:
The specification asks for the effect of lifestyle factors at three **levels**. The trick is to say what changes at *that* level.

- **Local**: more people in an area needing GP and hospital care; families caring for relatives; people off work in local businesses.
- **National**: the cost to the health service of treating these diseases; fewer people able to work, so less tax is paid; less money for other services.
- **Global**: obesity rising across the world, including in lower- and middle-income countries, while malnutrition from too little food continues in the poorest places; smoking falling in some countries and still common in others.

No numbers here are needed: an exam question that wants them will give them to you.

rows: demand on GPs and hospitals; carers; lost work
health service costs; less tax; fewer workers
props.title: Three levels

visuals.alt: A table of the effects of lifestyle factors at local, national and global level

check.prompt: Which is an effect at national level?
check.solution: The **health service's costs** are a national effect. Families and GP surgeries are local; the world is global.
options: higher costs for the national health service
a family caring for a relative
a local GP surgery being busier
obesity rising around the world

steps.title: Treating cardiovascular disease
steps.body:
There are three kinds of treatment, and the specification asks you to **evaluate** them.

**Life-long medication**
- **Statins** lower blood cholesterol, slowing the build-up of fatty deposits.
- **Anticoagulants**, such as warfarin, and antiplatelet drugs such as aspirin make clots less likely.
- **Antihypertensives** lower blood pressure.

**Surgical procedures**
- A **stent**, a mesh tube, holds a narrowed artery open.
- A **bypass** uses a blood vessel from elsewhere in the body to carry blood round a blockage.
- A **heart transplant** replaces a failing heart.

**Lifestyle changes**: stop smoking, eat less saturated fat and salt, exercise more, drink less alcohol.

visuals.alt: A table of the three types of treatment for cardiovascular disease with an advantage and a disadvantage of each

check.solution: A **stent** is a mesh tube that keeps the artery open so blood can flow.
options: holds a narrowed artery open
lowers cholesterol in the blood
stops the blood from clotting
replaces a damaged heart valve

steps.title: How to write an 'evaluate' answer
steps.body: *Evaluate* questions on cardiovascular treatments are usually six marks, marked by level. The top level needs **both sides of each treatment** and a **justified conclusion**. A plan helps.

visuals.problem: Evaluate the treatments for cardiovascular disease

steps.text: Medication: for — no operation; against — lifelong, side effects
steps.note: One for, one against, for each

steps.text: Surgery: for — quick, fixes a severe blockage; against — risks of infection and bleeding, recovery time
Lifestyle: for — cheap, no side effects, helps other diseases too; against — slow, depends on the person
Conclusion: it depends on severity — surgery for a severe blockage, lifestyle and medication for early risk; usually combined
steps.note: The judgement is where the top marks are

check.prompt: What must an *evaluate* answer include to reach the top level?
check.solution: *Evaluate* means weigh and **judge**. Without a conclusion the answer stops at the middle level.
options: a justified conclusion
a diagram of the heart
at least three calculations
a list of every medicine

steps.title: Your turn: BMI both ways
steps.body:
Try both of these before looking at the steps. The first is the straight calculation; the second is the rearranging that the harder questions ask for.

1. Mass 70 kg, height 1.75 m. What is the BMI?
2. What mass would give this person a BMI of 20?

steps.title: Going deeper: risk, levels and judgements
steps.body:
Three habits lift answers in this topic.

**Risk, not cause.** Write that smoking *increases the risk* of cardiovascular disease, and that non-communicable diseases come from *several factors interacting*. A study showing a link is evidence of a risk factor, not proof that everyone affected will get the disease.

**Say which level.** For local, national and global questions, name the level and give an effect that belongs to it — the health service budget is national, a busy GP surgery is local.

**Judge.** For treatments, weigh each one and conclude. The best conclusions depend on the patient: *for a severe blockage, surgery; for early risk, lifestyle and medication.*

And with BMI, know its limit: it cannot tell muscle from fat, which is why doctors also use the waist-to-hip ratio.

rows: surgery for severe blockage; else lifestyle
BMI cannot tell muscle from fat

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Non-communicable diseases** come from the **interaction of factors**: genes, lifestyle, environment, age. A **risk factor** raises the chance; it does not make a disease certain.
- **Diet and exercise**: energy in above energy used leads to **obesity**; **malnutrition** is any unbalanced diet, too little or too much.
- **BMI = mass (kg) ÷ height (m)²**. Adult bands: under 18.5, 18.5 to 24.9, 25 to 29.9, 30 or more. It cannot tell muscle from fat.
- **Waist-to-hip ratio = waist ÷ hip**: shows fat stored around the abdomen.
- **Alcohol** damages liver cells: **cirrhosis**, and a higher risk of liver cancer.
- **Smoking** damages artery linings, so fatty deposits narrow them; nicotine raises blood pressure; carbon monoxide cuts oxygen. Blocked coronary artery: heart attack.
- **Levels**: local, national, global — name the level and give an effect that belongs to it.
- **Treatments**: medication (statins, anticoagulants, for life), surgery (stents, bypass, transplant), lifestyle changes. Evaluate each and conclude.

questions.prompt: Which disease can be caused by drinking too much alcohol over many years?
questions.solution: Long-term heavy drinking damages liver cells, which are replaced by scar tissue: **cirrhosis**. The others are communicable diseases caused by pathogens.
options: cirrhosis of the liver
tuberculosis
malaria
cholera

Which lifestyle factor increases the risk of cardiovascular disease?
questions.solution: **Smoking** damages the lining of the arteries and raises blood pressure. The others lower risk or have no effect.
options: smoking
eating fruit and vegetables
regular exercise

questions.prompt: Name a surgical procedure used to treat a narrowed coronary artery.
questions.solution: A **stent** holds the artery open; a **bypass** routes blood around the blockage using a vessel from elsewhere in the body.

questions.prompt: A person's waist measures 84 cm and their hips 105 cm. Calculate their waist-to-hip ratio.
questions.solution: Ratio = waist ÷ hip = 84 ÷ 105 = **0.8**. Both in cm, so the units cancel.

questions.prompt: How does smoking increase the risk of a heart attack?
questions.solution: Chemicals in smoke **damage the lining of the arteries**; fatty deposits build up at the damage and narrow the coronary arteries, so heart muscle gets less oxygen. Carbon monoxide makes things worse by reducing the oxygen the blood carries, so the heart works harder, not slower.

markScheme.description: damage artery walls, fatty deposits narrow them

options: chemicals damage artery walls, so fatty deposits narrow them
nicotine kills heart muscle cells directly within minutes
tar blocks the coronary arteries by travelling in the blood
carbon monoxide makes the heart beat much more slowly

questions.solution: **Statins** lower blood cholesterol, which slows the build-up of fatty deposits in the arteries. They are taken for life.
options: lowers the level of cholesterol in the blood
dissolves a blood clot in the brain
widens the artery with a mesh tube
kills bacteria in the coronary arteries

questions.prompt: Explain how a stent treats coronary heart disease.
questions.solution: Three links: a stent is a mesh tube put into the narrowed coronary artery; it holds the artery open; so more blood reaches the heart muscle, which gets enough oxygen.

markScheme.description: a mesh tube inserted into the narrowed coronary artery
so blood, and oxygen, reach the heart muscle

criteria.text: A stent is a mesh tube placed in the narrowed coronary artery
So more blood, carrying oxygen, reaches the heart muscle

questions.modelAnswer: A stent is a small mesh tube that is put into the narrowed part of a coronary artery. It holds the artery open, so blood can flow through it freely again. That means the heart muscle receives enough oxygen, which reduces the risk of a heart attack.

questions.prompt: Many non-communicable diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors. What does this mean?
questions.solution: No single cause: **genes, lifestyle and environment** combine. That is why two people who both smoke can have very different outcomes.

markScheme.description: several factors combine to affect risk

options: several factors, such as genes and lifestyle, combine to affect risk
a single pathogen causes the disease by itself
the disease can be passed on through contact with others
the disease only develops in people over a certain age

questions.prompt: A person is 1.75 m tall and has a BMI of 24. Calculate their mass in kg.
Evaluate the use of medication, surgery and lifestyle changes to treat cardiovascular disease.
questions.solution: For each treatment an advantage and a disadvantage, then a judgement. Medication: no operation, but taken for life, with side effects. Surgery: fast and effective for a severe blockage, but risks of infection, bleeding and anaesthetic, and a recovery time. Lifestyle: cheap, no side effects, improves health overall, but slow, needs willpower, and not enough alone for severe disease. Judgement: depends on how severe; often combined.

markScheme.description: Level 2 (3 to 4): advantages and disadvantages of at least two
Level 3 (5 to 6): all three weighed, with a justified conclusion

criteria.text: Medication weighed: no operation, but lifelong, with side effects
Surgery weighed: fast for severe blockages, but risks and recovery
Lifestyle weighed, and a justified conclusion

questions.modelAnswer: **Medication** such as statins, which lower cholesterol, and anticoagulants, which reduce clotting, avoids an operation, but it has to be taken for life and can have side effects. **Surgery**, such as fitting a stent or a bypass, works quickly and can restore blood flow through a badly blocked artery, but every operation carries risks of infection, bleeding and reactions to the anaesthetic, and needs recovery time. **Lifestyle changes** — stopping smoking, eating less saturated fat, exercising more — are cheap and have no side effects, and they reduce the risk of other diseases too, but they take a long time to work and depend on the person keeping them up. The best choice depends on how severe the disease is: someone with a severe blockage needs surgery quickly, while someone at early risk may manage with lifestyle changes and medication. In practice they are usually combined, because lifestyle changes help every treatment work better.

questions.prompt: A rugby player has a BMI of 31, which is in the obese range, but very little body fat. Why?
questions.solution: BMI uses only mass and height, so it cannot tell **muscle from fat**. A very muscular person can be classed as obese while being very lean. Muscle is denser than fat, so it takes up *less* space for its mass.

markScheme.description: BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat

options: BMI does not tell muscle apart from fat
BMI is only accurate for people under 18
rugby players tend to be shorter than most
muscle takes up more space than fat does

questions.prompt: The number of people with obesity in a country is rising. Explain the effects this could have on the country as a whole.
questions.solution: National-level effects, each explained: more obesity-related disease (type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease); so more cost to the health service; more people too ill to work, so less money earned and less paid in tax; so less money for other services.

markScheme.description: more cost to the health service
so less tax income or less money for other services

criteria.text: More cases of diseases linked to obesity
Greater cost to the health service
Fewer people well enough to work
So less tax income, or less money for other services

questions.modelAnswer: More people with obesity means more cases of diseases linked to it, such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Treating them costs the national health service more, in medication, operations and hospital time. Some people will be too ill to work, so the country loses their work and the tax they would pay, which leaves less money for other services such as schools.

questions.prompt: A person has a mass of 90 kg and a height of 1.80 m. How much mass would they need to lose to reach a BMI of 25?
questions.solution: Mass at BMI 25 = 25 × 1.80² = 25 × 3.24 = 81 kg. They need to lose 90 − 81 = **9 kg**. (Their BMI now is 90 ÷ 3.24 = 27.8.)

questions.prompt: A study finds that people who drink more alcohol have more liver disease. Which statement is the best conclusion?
questions.solution: Alcohol is a **risk factor**: it makes liver disease more likely without guaranteeing it, and other factors — genes, diet, viral hepatitis — also play a part. That is the interaction of factors in 5.23.
options: Alcohol raises the risk of liver disease but does not make it certain
Everyone who drinks alcohol will develop liver disease one day
Liver disease makes people want to drink more alcohol than before
Alcohol is the only factor that causes all liver disease cases

questions.prompt: Suggest why a doctor might measure a patient's waist-to-hip ratio as well as their BMI.
questions.solution: BMI cannot tell muscle from fat; the ratio shows where fat is stored; fat around the waist is linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes.

markScheme.description: BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat
waist-to-hip ratio shows fat stored around the abdomen
which is linked to higher risk of cardiovascular disease or diabetes

criteria.text: BMI cannot tell muscle from fat
The ratio shows how much fat is stored around the waist
Fat there is linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease or type 2 diabetes

questions.modelAnswer: BMI uses only mass and height, so it cannot tell muscle from fat and can mislead for very muscular people. The waist-to-hip ratio shows how much fat is stored around the abdomen. Fat stored there is linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes, so the two measurements together give a better picture of risk.

questions.prompt: A patient's coronary artery is badly blocked and they have chest pain even when resting. Which treatment is most likely to help quickly?
questions.solution: With a severe blockage, blood flow has to be restored **quickly**, and surgery does that. Diet and exercise help but take months. Antibiotics treat bacterial infections, not blocked arteries.
options: a stent or bypass surgery
eating less saturated fat
taking more regular exercise
a course of antibiotics

questions.prompt: Obesity is rising around the world, yet malnutrition is still a global problem. How can both be true?
questions.solution: **Malnutrition** means an unbalanced diet: too little food or too little of some nutrients in some places, while elsewhere people take in more energy than they use and become obese. Both happen at the global level at once, sometimes in the same country.

markScheme.description: too little food for some, too much energy for others

options: Some people lack enough food while others eat more energy than they use
Obesity and malnutrition are two names for exactly the same condition
Malnutrition only affects people who are also obese at the same time
Global food supplies fell sharply, so everyone now eats far too little

questions.prompt: Explain how drinking too much alcohol over many years can lead to liver disease.
questions.solution: The liver breaks down alcohol, which is toxic; over time liver cells are damaged and die; they are replaced by scar tissue (cirrhosis), so the liver cannot work properly, and the risk of liver cancer rises.

markScheme.description: the liver breaks down alcohol, a toxin
liver cells are damaged or killed
replaced by scar tissue (cirrhosis), so the liver cannot work, or liver cancer

criteria.text: The liver breaks down alcohol, which is toxic
Liver cells are damaged and killed over time
Scar tissue replaces them (cirrhosis), so the liver fails, or cancer develops

questions.modelAnswer: The liver breaks down alcohol, which is a toxin. Drinking too much over many years damages and kills liver cells. They are replaced by scar tissue, which is called cirrhosis, so the liver can no longer do its jobs properly. Heavy drinking also increases the risk of liver cancer.

examTechnique.body:
Expect a calculation, an explanation and an evaluation from this topic. The calculations are BMI and the waist-to-hip ratio: square the height before dividing, rearrange confidently when the question gives the BMI and asks for mass, and remember that a ratio has no units. The explanations are chains — smoking to damaged arteries to narrowing to heart attack; alcohol to liver cell damage to cirrhosis.

The evaluation is usually the six-mark question on treatments for cardiovascular disease. Give an advantage and a disadvantage for each of medication, surgery and lifestyle change, then a conclusion that depends on the patient. Throughout, use the language of risk: lifestyle factors increase the risk of a disease; they do not cause it in everyone.
examinerErrors: Dividing by the height instead of the height squared when calculating BMI.
Writing that smoking *causes* heart disease, rather than increasing the risk.
Describing the three treatments without weighing them or reaching a conclusion.
Giving a local effect when the question asks for national or global.
Saying a stent lowers cholesterol, or a statin opens the artery: the two are often swapped.
Treating malnutrition as meaning only too little food.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer calculates BMI and the waist-to-hip ratio cleanly, including rearranging BMI to find a mass, and knows that BMI cannot tell muscle from fat. It explains how smoking and alcohol lead to disease as causal chains, uses the language of risk factors and interacting causes, and places each effect at the right level. On treatments it weighs medication, surgery and lifestyle change and reaches a conclusion that depends on how severe the disease is.
